item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for hyping up security risks of mainland apps
item.description:
Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for hyping up security risks of mainland apps Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-01-29
BEIJING, Jan. 28 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for hyping up the so-called information security risks of applications from the mainland. Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, stated at a press conference that the DPP moves have deprived people in Taiwan, especially the youth, of their right to know and the freedom to use social networking platforms. Noting that such moves reveal the fear and insecurity of the DPP authorities, Zhang said they will have to face the dire consequences of their wayward actions.

item.title: Chinese mainland spokesperson slams Lai Ching-te's flattering remarks on Japan
item.description:
Chinese mainland spokesperson slams Lai Ching-te's flattering remarks on Japan Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-02-11
BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday denounced Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te for ignoring the heinous crimes committed by Japan during its colonial rule over Taiwan, describing their flattering remarks toward Japan as utterly disgraceful. Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to a media inquiry about Lai's intention to work with Japan to "deal with regional challenges." Zhu also urged the Japanese side to retract Sanae Takaichi's erroneous remarks on Taiwan, handle Taiwan-related issues prudently, and abide by the one-China principle with concrete actions. item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges
item.description: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson has condemned Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for imposing restrictions and obstacles on cross-Strait exchanges in pursuit of their "Taiwan independence" agenda and selfish gains. The DPP authorities, led by Lai Ching-te, are the biggest obstacle to cross-Strait interactions and their acts have drawn strong criticism from various sectors in Taiwan, Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular press briefing on Wednesday. Zhu expressed the hope that Taiwan compatriots will firmly oppose the retrogressive actions of the DPP authorities and promote exchanges and cooperation across the Taiwan Strait in various fields. She noted that cross-Strait flight routes have been disrupted due to interference from the DPP authorities, with previously operated destinations yet to resume normal operations. In 2025, the average passenger load factor on cross-Strait routes reached 80 percent, reflecting the strong need for direct flights between the two sides of the Strait, Zhu said. "We hope that the Taiwan side will heed public opinion and lift unreasonable restrictions on cross-Strait air transport as soon as possible," she added.

item.title: One-China support narrows DPP agenda
item.description: One-China support narrows DPP agenda CAI MENG/CHINA DAILY Editor's note:The Taiwan question is a key focus for China and the international community. China Daily is publishing a series of reports to track hot Taiwan-related topics and address disinformation from the Democratic Progressive Party administration. The frequent reaffirmation of the one-China principle by countries around the world has highlighted the gap between the Democratic Progressive Party authorities' claims of international support for their separatist agenda and the official positions of most sovereign states, analysts and officials said. They said the DPP authorities' pursuit of a "Taiwan independence" separatist agenda, in defiance of the widely recognized one-China principle, has become the fundamental obstacle to Taiwan's proper participation in international activities. In recent weeks, several countries have reiterated their commitment to the one-China principle through diplomatic engagements and official statements, reaffirming that their relations with China are based on this fundamental position. On Aug 5, Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale said in an address to the National Parliament that relations with China are of vital importance to the country's development, reaffirming that his government will continue to uphold the one-China principle. During Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul's visit to China from July 16 to 20, he said Thailand firmly adheres to the one-China policy and will never support any "Taiwan independence" activities. A joint statement issued by the two governments on July 20 said Thailand supports China's efforts to achieve peaceful reunification and opposes "Taiwan independence" in any form. On July 16, Papua New Guinea Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko said in a social media post that his country had reaffirmed its one-China policy and would close the "Chinese Taipei Economic Office" in Papua New Guinea. During Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi's visits to Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Norway from July 2 to 7, the four Nordic countries reiterated their adherence to the one-China principle, which they said serves as an important political foundation for developing bilateral relations with China. Cambodia also reaffirmed its position after the DPP authorities announced the suspension of so-called visa facilitation measures for Cambodian citizens. The Cambodian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said that Cambodia regards Taiwan as part of China and will not change its long-standing position of upholding the one-China principle. The repeated reaffirmations came as the DPP authorities have accused the mainland of using international exchanges to "diminish Taiwan's status". In response, Chen Binhua, spokesman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a news conference in July that "Taiwan independence" separatist activities have no future and are increasingly heading toward a dead end. He stressed that the one-China principle is a prevailing consensus of the international community and a fundamental norm governing international relations. Zhu Guilan, an assistant professor at Tsinghua University's Institute for Taiwan Studies, said the DPP authorities have taken isolated unofficial interactions and remarks by individual politicians in certain countries and portrayed them as evidence of so-called international support for Taiwan. "Such claims stand in stark contrast to the official positions of sovereign countries around the world," she said, adding that the DPP's narrative on "Taiwan independence" lacks a foundation in reality and has continued to lose credibility. So far, 183 countries worldwide have established diplomatic relations with China on the basis of the one-China principle. The principle is based on three key elements: There is only one China in the world; Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory; and the government of the People's Republic of China is the sole legitimate government representing the whole of China, according to China's Position Paper on United Nations General Assembly Resolution 2758. According to the Chinese Foreign Ministry, the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 represented a change of government, not a change in China's sovereignty or territorial integrity. Taiwan, which was returned to China after Japan's colonial rule ended in 1945, remains part of China, the ministry said. In 1971, the 26th session of the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758, which restored the lawful rights of the People's Republic of China in the UN and recognized the representatives of the PRC government as the only legitimate representatives of China at the UN. Following the adoption of the resolution, the UN Secretariat began using the designation "Taiwan, Province of China" in official records and documents when referring to the island. "Upholding the core principles of the UN Charter, including sovereign equality and non-interference in internal affairs, the one-China principle has gained broad recognition from the international community and has become a basic norm governing international relations that cannot be challenged," Zhu said. The one-China principle has also been reflected in bilateral diplomatic documents between China and other countries. Zhu said some external forces, driven by geopolitical interests, have attempted to create an impression of support for Taiwan through unofficial exchanges, visits by lawmakers and civil activities. The DPP authorities, she added, have deliberately amplified such signals and used them for political purposes on the island. "The repeated and explicit reaffirmation of the one-China principle by countries around the world demonstrates that most members of the international community do not support attempts by certain external forces to use the Taiwan question to contain China or create tensions across the Taiwan Strait," she said. Such a stance, she added, has further exposed the lack of international support for the DPP's separatist narrative. Zhu said these countries' firm adherence to the one-China principle has narrowed the channels through which the DPP authorities seek to expand their so-called international space, and weakened their hopes of relying on external forces to interfere in cross-Strait affairs. DPP strategy After the DPP came into office in 2016 with its "Taiwan independence" separatist agenda, its refusal to recognize the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, led to escalating tensions across the Taiwan Strait. Since then, the DPP authorities have pursued various channels to expand Taiwan's "international space", including unofficial visits and civil exchange events. These efforts have been criticized by the mainland as attempts to seek external support for a separatist agenda. However, despite these efforts, Taiwan's international space has continued to shrink under the DPP's rule, as countries around the world have maintained their commitment to the one-China principle. In May, the 79th World Health Assembly decided not to include a proposal to invite Taiwan to participate in the WHA as an observer on its agenda, marking the 10th consecutive year that a Taiwan-related proposal has failed to pass. The Chinese Foreign Ministry and China's Permanent Mission to the UN Office at Geneva said the decision was made because the Taiwan authorities have persisted in their separatist position of pursuing "Taiwan independence". From 2009 to 2016, when the Chinese Kuomintang was in office and adhered to the 1992 Consensus, Taiwan participated in the WHA as an observer under the name "Chinese Taipei" for eight consecutive years, based on consensus reached between the mainland and Taiwan. Meanwhile, since 2016, 10 countries, including Panama, the Solomon Islands, Nicaragua and Honduras, have successively severed their so-called diplomatic ties with the Taiwan authorities and established diplomatic relations with China. While the DPP authorities have repeatedly accused the mainland of "suppressing" Taiwan's international participation and portrayed themselves as "victims" in an attempt to gain external support, Zhu said the fundamental reason for Taiwan's difficulties in expanding its international engagement lies in the authorities' obstinate separatist stance of pursuing "Taiwan independence". Recent developments have further illustrated this trend. South Africa recently listed Taiwan as "Taiwan, China" in its electronic visa system. Earlier, the South African government had downgraded Taiwan's representative office and required it to relocate from Pretoria, the country's administrative capital. The DPP authorities protested the moves. In March, after Cameroon designated Taiwan as "Taiwan, Province of China" in its visa system, Taiwan's external affairs department announced that it would not participate in the 14th World Trade Organization Ministerial Conference held in Yaounde, the capital of Cameroon. In April, Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar revoked overflight permissions for Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te's planned transit during his visit to Eswatini. The decision resulted in the cancellation of Lai's trip. On May 2, Lai later traveled secretly by air to Eswatini, a move described by some media outlets as "diplomacy by stealth". Cheng Li-wun, chairwoman of the KMT, also questioned Lai's approach, saying that the international community accepts the 1992 Consensus and does not support "Taiwan independence". "Why does the DPP insist on going its own way, leading to repeated setbacks and leaving the island in a difficult situation?" Cheng said after Lai's planned trip was disrupted. Way forward Zhu said the mainland has always supported Taiwan's participation in international activities related to people's livelihoods under the one-China principle. However, she noted that the DPP authorities' repeated attempts to pursue "de jure independence" through international affairs and challenge the international consensus have made it increasingly difficult for Taiwan to gain access to relevant channels for international participation. Public opinion on the island has also criticized the DPP authorities' approach to external relations. Following Lai's visit to Eswatini, reports revealed that Taiwan planned to invest NT$25 billion ($775 million) in the country. Opposition parties and commentators in Taiwan questioned the move, saying the authorities had overlooked pressing livelihood issues at home while providing large amounts of financial support overseas. Zhu said the few remaining "diplomatic allies" maintained through the DPP's "dollar diplomacy" have a fragile foundation. Meanwhile, years of lobbying efforts and protest campaigns have failed to help Taiwan secure observer status at the WHA. "Such actions are essentially political stunts driven by the 'Taiwan independence' agenda and cannot secure stable participation rights for Taiwan in international organizations," she said. Zhu said only by abandoning the separatist stance and returning to the 1992 Consensus can cross-Strait relations return to healthy interaction, enabling Taiwan to achieve sustainable and meaningful participation in international affairs based on the one-China principle.

item.title: Taiwan groups warn of Taiwan Strait security risks due to Japan's neo-militarism
item.description: Taiwan groups warn of Taiwan Strait security risks due to Japan's neo-militarism TAIPEI, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- Several Taiwan-based groups have voiced opposition to Japan's neo-militarism, warning that Tokyo's push for a greater military role in regional affairs could undermine peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait and throughout East Asia. Their concerns were expressed at forums, seminars and a public gathering held on Friday and Saturday, as Aug. 15 this year marks the 81st anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II. At a forum in Taipei, more than 10 organizations, including the Reunification Alliance Party, brought together scholars and experts from both sides of the Taiwan Strait, as well as from Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Japan and Australia. Participants called on people on both sides of the Strait and across Asia to draw lessons from history, oppose the expansionist ambitions of Japanese right-wing forces, and safeguard peace and stability in East Asia. Citing remarks previously made by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Wang Yung, president of the Reunification Alliance Party and host of the forum, said they suggested the possibility of Japan's military intervention in Taiwan-related affairs and represented a key sign of the country's accelerating remilitarization. The Japanese government was seeking to loosen the constraints imposed by its pacifist Constitution and the long-standing post-war principle of an "exclusively defense-oriented policy," Wang noted, warning that such moves could have serious repercussions for security in the Taiwan Strait and peace in East Asia. A seminar was also held on Saturday in Taichung, central Taiwan, drawing over 30 descendants of resistance fighters who fought against Japanese aggression, as well as historians, teachers and students. The event was jointly organized by several Taiwan-based groups, including an association representing relatives of patriots who fought against Japanese aggression. Li Su-hui, daughter of anti-Japanese resistance fighter Li Tsang-chiang, said her family retained painful memories of resistance to Japanese colonial rule in Taiwan from 1895 to 1945. "Remembering history is not merely about paying tribute to those who came before us, but also about passing on the spirit of resistance from generation to generation," Li said. She voiced concern over the resurgence of Japanese right-wing forces and signs of militarism re-emerging, saying the seminar could help young people develop a proper understanding of their national identity and history. "We are part of the Chinese nation, and the lessons of history must not be forgotten," Li said. Shaw Kai-ping, also a descendant of an anti-Japanese resistance fighter, warned of the risks posed by both a revival of Japanese militarism and growing secessionist activities in Taiwan. "At a time when the Democratic Progressive Party authorities are vigorously promoting a secessionist narrative, we need to stand up and help more people in Taiwan recognize that our motherland is China and our ancestral homeland is on the Chinese mainland," he said. On Friday, several civic groups, such as the Reunification Alliance Party and the Labor Party, gathered and protested outside the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association in Taipei. Wu Jung-yuan, chairman of the Labor Party, said Japan's war of aggression against China had caused more than 35 million Chinese casualties, while Taiwan endured 50 years of Japanese colonial rule, inflicting profound suffering on people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. "Taiwan is part of China," Wu said, calling on people on both sides of the Strait to work together to oppose external interference, safeguard peace and stability across the Strait, and strive for national reunification.

item.title: Mainland condemns DPP for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges
item.description: Mainland condemns DPP for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges BEIJING, Aug. 19 (Xinhua) -- A mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for creating obstacles to cross-Strait exchanges and misleading the public with false claims. Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks at a press conference in response to questions concerning recent moves by the DPP authorities to restrict or discourage exchanges with the mainland. Responding to claims by Taiwan's mainland affairs council that the new mainland entry and exit regulations could pose risks to Taiwan residents traveling to or working on the mainland, Zhu said there was no need for Taiwan residents to worry. The regulations are mainly aimed at improving the system for preventing security risks related to outbound travel and ensuring that reasons given in entry and exit applications are truthful and lawful, Zhu said. The regulations will help protect the legitimate rights and interests of people engaged in cross-Strait exchanges while creating a better legal environment for Taiwan residents visiting the mainland, she added. The DPP authorities are deliberately exaggerating risks with ill intent and seeking to obstruct cross-Strait exchanges through intimidation, misinformation and other means, Zhu said. She also rejected claims by Taiwan authorities that a mainland public service platform for young people from Taiwan was intended to collect personal information or serve political purposes. The DPP authorities were deliberately smearing the platform while restricting information and opportunities available to young people from Taiwan, said the spokesperson. "The trend of closer cross-Strait exchanges cannot be stopped," Zhu said, stressing that young people from Taiwan should have the right to choose where they pursue development opportunities. On the seizure by Taiwan authorities of a motorcycle assembled in Taiwan from parts of a mainland-made ZXMOTO motorcycle, Zhu said the move reflected the DPP authorities' efforts to block high-quality mainland products from entering Taiwan. Such actions run counter to the wishes of the people and will only undermine the island's business environment, Zhu added. Interest in ZXMOTO surged across Taiwan after the company's 820RR-RS race bike swept two races at the Portuguese round of the Superbike World Championship in March. Under current Taiwan regulations, however, complete heavy motorcycles and engines from the Chinese mainland are prohibited from entering Taiwan. Zhang Xue, founder of ZXMOTO, has previously expressed strong interest in opening a store in Taiwan, but the DPP authorities publicly opposed the proposal.

item.title: 8th "Guangming Cup" Cross-Strait Slow-Pitch Softball Friendship Invitational Kicks Off
item.description:
8th "Guangming Cup" Cross-Strait Slow-Pitch Softball Friendship Invitational Kicks Off Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-14
Aug 14(Taiwan.cn)—Under the theme "One Ball, One Heart Across the Strait," the 8th "Guangming Cup" Cross-Strait Slow-Pitch Softball Friendship Invitational Tournament was held from August 8 to 9 at the softball fields of Guangming Science Park and the High School Affiliated to the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Guangming District, Shenzhen. A total of 10 teams with around 180 players from the Chinese mainland, Taiwan, and Hong Kong gathered in Guangming. United by softball, they took part in this vibrant cross-Strait event that fosters shared aspirations. The competition venue buzzed with excitement and youthful energy. Amid flying red clay, players from both sides of Taiwan Strait swung bats, made diving catches, and sprinted at full speed, drawing cheers from spectators with every brilliant play. On the pitcher's mound, pitchers kept opponents in check with precise pitching. In the batter's box, batters swung hard, sending balls soaring toward the outfield. Base runners raced swiftly between bases in fierce competition. The stadium brimmed with dynamism and passion. The "Guangming Cup" Slow-Pitch Softball Tournament is committed to promoting exchanges and integration between compatriots across the Taiwan Strait. Using softball as a signature platform, it deepens interactions among young people from both sides and facilitates cultural exchange and mutual understanding. It fully demonstrates the innovative vitality, ecological appeal, and human warmth of Guangming Science City. The event continues to establish itself as a distinguished brand for cross-Strait sports and cultural exchanges in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. Every swing of the bat conveys the profound bond between compatriots and the heartwarming power of pursuing dreams side by side. (Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Shenzhen) Related Stories

item.title: Zhong Family from Taiwan Fulfills Decades-Old Dream of Ancestral Root-Searching in Jiaoling
item.description: Zhong Family from Taiwan Fulfills Decades-Old Dream of Ancestral Root-Searching in Jiaoling Aug 14(Taiwan.cn)—In August 2026, Zhong Ronghe and his son Zhong Binghan, a father and son from Kaohsiung, Taiwan, crossed the Strait to visit their ancestral home in Jiaoling County, Meizhou, Guangdong, and worship their ancestors. They fulfilled their family’s decades-long aspiration to trace their origins and pay homage to their forebears. In April this year, Zhong Binghan, who had just returned from studies in the United Kingdom, made his first solo trip to Jiaoling, following his father’s request to trace their ancestral roots. With assistance from the local Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office and clan relatives, cross-checking of genealogical records confirmed Guangfu Town as their ancestral hometown. Zhong Binghan then offered incense and paid homage at Yixuan Ancestral Hall and Yangting Ancestral Hall. He shared the good news via video call with his father in Taiwan, fulfilling Zhong Ronghe’s long-cherished wish to trace his roots.

item.title: The Taiwan Affairs Office of Shangcheng County Organizes Intangible Cultural Heritage Experience Activity for Taiwan-Related Families
item.description: Aug 14(Taiwan.cn)—On August 13, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Shangcheng County, Henan Province, organized local Taiwan-related families to take part in an experience activity of grass-beating printing, an intangible cultural heritage. Taking traditional intangible cultural heritage as a bridge, the event allowed family members of Taiwan compatriots to appreciate the beauty of folk craftsmanship up close. Through immersive hands-on practice, it fostered kinship and friendship and deepened cross-Strait cultural bonds The activity site was immersed in a warm atmosphere. Inheritors of the intangible cultural heritage gave detailed lectures on the origin, cultural implications and inheritance value of grass-beating printing, and demonstrated the full operational procedures in a hands on manner. During the experience, parents and children from Taiwan-related families worked side by side in close coordination, carefully completing every procedure. Participants experienced the ingenuity and charm of the traditional craft through hands-on practice. One after another, unique grass-rubbing prints with varied patterns were finished. Their simple and natural patterns embodied the charm of traditional culture and deep local affection. This intangible cultural heritage experience has innovated forms of cross-Strait exchanges and enriched the cultural life of Taiwan-related families. Rooted in culture and hometown sentiment, the activity helped advance the influence of fine traditional Chinese culture. It subtly enhanced Taiwan-related families’ cultural identity and sense of belonging to the motherland, further promoted emotional rapport between compatriots across the Strait, and consolidated the emotional and cultural foundation for people-to-people exchanges and integration across the Taiwan Strait. (Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Xinyang and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Shangcheng)

item.title: For 14 Consecutive Years, Taiwan-Based Compatriot Grants Heartwarming Scholarship to Hometown Students
item.description:
For 14 Consecutive Years, Taiwan-Based Compatriot Grants Heartwarming Scholarship to Hometown Students Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-14
Aug 14(Taiwan.cn)—On August 13, the awarding ceremony for the "Tao Yuebo Hometown Youth Scholarship" was held at No. 2 High School of Xinzhou District, Wuhan. Tao Deyou, a Taiwan-based compatriot originally from Xinzhou, once again provided financial aid to college-bound students from his hometown, continuing an unbroken cross-Strait act of kindness for 14 years. At the ceremony, Tao Deyou, accompanied by his family, personally presented scholarships to seven eligible students this year, each receiving 4,000 yuan. While handing over the red envelopes, he urged the young recipients: "Study hard in college and grow into individuals who contribute to society." Tao Jun, Tao Deyou's niece, drove over 100 kilometers from Huangshi to attend the event and gave each scholarship recipient a custom-made red insulated mug. Staff members from the Huangshi Port-Area Committee of the Revolutionary Committee of the Chinese Kuomintang also offered each student a 500-yuan travel subsidy. Born in Taiwan, Tao Deyou pursued business careers in Hong Kong, South Africa, and elsewhere before retiring. During a trip back to his ancestral home in 2013, he learned that his grandfather had served as a school director of Zhengyuan Middle School, the predecessor of No. 2 High School of Xinzhou. In honor of his great-uncle, Tao Yuebo, he established the scholarship to support financially disadvantaged students admitted to universities. Despite the distance across the Taiwan Strait, this annual August promise has never faltered for 14 years. To date, more than 100 underprivileged students from No. 1, No. 2, and No. 4 High Schools of Xinzhou have benefited from the fund. Related Stories
